newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia deeply isolated as Tudjman starts new term.
newsitem.headline: Croatia deeply isolated as Tudjman starts new term.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman, sworn in for another five-year term on Tuesday, now faces the difficult task of hauling Croatia out of international isolation and tackling social discontent at home.

The 76-year-old president, who led Croatia's split from federal Yugoslavia in 1991, took the oath a week before officially taking office, on a day commemorating a victory over minority Serbs who opposed Croatia's independence.

The former Yugoslav army general must now prove himself capable of achieving peacetime goals, although his inauguration speech gave little indication that Croatia's policies would substantially change.

"We strive towards integration into the Euro-Atlantic economic and security associations," Tudjman declared, restating what has been a cornerstone of his programme since winning the first democratic elections in 1990.

But Croatia, which dreams of joining the European Union and NATO, has never before been so isolated -- not even during its involvement in a Croat-Moslem war in Bosnia, when the world almost slapped international sanctions on Zagreb.
Western diplomats are twisting Tudjman's arm to make him honour peace commitments he assumed in 1995 peace accords, which ended the wars in Croatia and Bosnia.

While renewing verbal support for the Bosnian peace and the fragile Croat-Moslem federation there, Tudjman added: "Croatia will not give in to pressures, nor will it make concessions that would be harmful to its national security or sovereignty."

The peace accords require Zagreb to hand over indicted Bosnian Croats to an international war crimes tribunal, allow the return of all Serb war refugees, and quell nationalist Bosnian Croat opposition to the Croat-Moslem federation.

Croatia handed over one war crimes suspect while another turned himself in, but Zagreb has failed to ensure all Serbs can return in safety. The West unprecedentedly made the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank withdraw promised funds this summer.
"Croatia is one of the most prosperous of the former socialist countries... It is now attractive to foreign investors," Tudjman insisted.
His first chance to iron out some of the critical issues will come at a meeting on Wednesday with the president of Bosnia's collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, at the Adriatic port of Split.

Also present will be U.S. diplomat Richard Holbrooke, returning to the Balkans to exert pressure on all parties for faster implementation of the peace accord he engineered in 1995. If the talks collapse, Zagreb could be dragged into further isolation.
But Tudjman is likely to score at least one victory, by completing the reintegration to Croatia of the last Serb-populated enclave of Eastern Slavonia.

United Nations administration of the enclave is set to end in January, when a large-scale return of Croat and Serb refugees should gain momentum. "It will require strong moral leadership of Tudjman and his government," a U.N. official said.
"This is the last chapter in the victorious conclusion to the war," Tudjman said, adding that Croatia could now dedicate itself to reconstruction and rebuilding of its economy.
"We shall strive to raise employment and Gross Domestic Product... We have to ensure better living standards."

The main domestic threat to Tudjman's rule is smouldering dissatisfaction among a majority of Croats who are struggling to make ends meet. At the same time, hasty privatisation has created a small, enormously rich elite closely linked to his ruling party.

"In my new mandate I will demand consistency in the fight against corruption... I will even more resolutely insist on removing all remnants of the communist regime," the president said, to a huge applause from the crowd.
